content: The collaboration between Makerere University and Johns Hopkins University (MU-JHU) in Uganda involves researchers such as Pamela Nabeta from FIND in Switzerland, Claudia M. Denkinger and Mary Gaeddert from the University of Heidelberg in Germany, and others. Additionally, contributors from the Elizabeth Glaser Pediatric AIDS Foundation in Switzerland include Sushant Mukherjee, Mario J.P. Songane, Jean-François Lemaire, and Martina Casenghi. Nyashadzaishe Mafirakureva and Peter J. Dodd from the University of Sheffield in the United Kingdom, as well as Nancy Medley and Melissa Taylor from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, also participated in this effort. Susanna S. van Wyk from Stellenbosch University in South Africa contributed to the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (Module 5: Management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents). Sandy Oliver, affiliated with University College London in the United Kingdom and the University of Johannesburg in South Africa, and Joanna Orne-Gliemann from Université de Bordeaux in France, were also involved. The WHO Guidelines Steering Group included Annabel Baddeley, Lice Gonzalez Angulo, Ernesto Jaramillo, Avinash Kanchar, and Charalambos Sismanidis from the WHO Global Tuberculosis Programme. Martina Penazzato from the WHO Global HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infections Programme, Bernadette Cappello and Lorenzo Moja from the WHO Department of Health Products, Policy, and Standards, and Marie Valentin from the WHO Department of Regulation and Prequalification also contributed. Corinne Simone Collette Merle from the WHO Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases, Valentina Baltag and Wilson Milton Were from the WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child & Adolescent Health & Ageing, Lina Mahy from the WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, and Chiara Servili from the WHO Department of Mental Health and Substance Use were part of the team. Sarah Rylance from the WHO Department of Non-Communicable Diseases Management, Ogtay Gozalov from the WHO Regional Office for Europe, Mukta Sharma from the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia, Kyung Hyun Oh from the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific Region, Pedro Avedillo from the Pan American Health Organization, Kenza Bennani and Martin van den Boom from the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean Region, and André Ndongosieme from the WHO Regional Office for Africa also participated. Other contributors included Pete Dodd from Sheffield University in the United Kingdom, Anneke Hesseling from Stellenbosch University in South Africa, Oliver Marcy from the University of Bordeaux in France, Nicole Salazar-Austin from Johns Hopkins University in the United States, and James Seddon from Imperial College London in England. These individuals served as technical resource persons during the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting. Observers at the GDG meeting included Draurio Barreira Cravo Neto from Unitaid in Switzerland, Charlotte Colvin from USAID in the United States, Anne Detjen from UNICEF in the United States, Thomas Gradel from Unitaid in Switzerland, Brian Kaiser from the Stop TB Partnership Global Drug Facility in Switzerland, Michael McCaul from Stellenbosch University in South Africa, Lawrence Mbuagbaw from St. Joseph’s Healthcare in Canada, Celeste Naude from Stellenbosch University in South Africa, Oxana Rucsineanu from the TB Community Advisory Board, Anna Scardigli from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria in Switzerland, and Cherise Scott from Unitaid. The WHO Global Tuberculosis Programme expressed gratitude to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee for their review and approval of the guidelines. This update was funded by grants provided to WHO by Unitaid and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). Abbreviations: AIDS: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome ANC: Antenatal Care ART: Antiretroviral Therapy BCG: Bacille Calmette-Guérin CALHIV: Children (and Adolescents) Living with HIV Infection CHW: Community Health Worker CXR: Chest X-ray or Chest Radiography DR-TB: Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis DS-TB: Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis DST: Drug Susceptibility Testing DTG: Dolutegravir EP-TB: Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis FDC: Fixed-Dose Combination (medicines) GDG: Guideline Development Group GRADE: Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus IGRA: Interferon-Gamma Release Assay MDR-TB: Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis TB: Tuberculosis WHO: World Health Organization XDR-TB: Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Definitions: Active Tuberculosis Case-Finding: This refers to provider-initiated screening and testing in communities, often utilizing mobile X-ray units and rapid molecular tests. It is sometimes used interchangeably with systematic screening. Advanced HIV Disease: For adolescents and children aged 5 years and older, this is defined as a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/mm³ or a WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 event at presentation for care. All children under 5 years living with HIV are considered to have advanced disease at presentation. Adverse Event: Any untoward medical occurrence in a person with TB during treatment with a pharmaceutical product, which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment. Age Groups: Infants are defined as those under 1 year of age, children as those under 10 years, and adolescents as those aged 10–19 years. Adults are individuals aged 20 years or older. Bacteriologically Confirmed Tuberculosis: TB diagnosed in a biological specimen using a WHO-approved rapid test, smear microscopy, or culture. Contact Investigation: A systematic process to identify individuals, including children and adolescents, with undiagnosed TB disease or infection among the contacts of an index TB patient. Decentralization: The provision of TB services for children and adolescents at lower levels of the health system, such as district hospitals or primary healthcare facilities, to improve access and outcomes. Differentiated HIV Service Delivery Model: A person-centered approach to simplify HIV service provision across the care cascade, tailored to the needs of people living with HIV while reducing unnecessary burdens on the health system. Extensive Pulmonary Tuberculosis Disease: Characterized by bilateral cavitary disease or extensive parenchymal damage on chest radiography. In children under 15 years, it is typically defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on imaging. Family-Centered, Integrated Care: Care models that prioritize the needs, values, and preferences of the child or adolescent and their family, incorporating health education, communication, and psychological support. Integrated Treatment Decision Algorithm: A flowchart that assigns evidence-based scores to microbiological, clinical, and radiological features to guide clinicians in initiating TB treatment in children.
